The Master Answer: In CMOS technology, a NAND gate has NMOS transistors in series (pull-down) and PMOS transistors in parallel (pull-up). A NOR gate has PMOS transistors in series (pull-up) and NMOS transistors in parallel. In silicon crystal, electron mobility in NMOS (\mu_n pprox 1350\text{ cm}^2/\text{V}\cdot\text{s}) is 2.5 to 3 times higher than hole mobility in PMOS (\mu_p pprox 480\text{ cm}^2/\text{V}\cdot\text{s}). Therefore, series PMOS transistors in a NOR gate must be made 2.5 to 3 times wider to achieve equal rise time, dramatically increasing parasitic gate capacitance, silicon die area, and propagation delay! Consequently, CMOS NAND gates are significantly faster, occupy much less silicon area, and consume less dynamic power than CMOS NOR gates.

Quadrants II and IV are the braking quadrants: the machine acts as a generator and the drive must have somewhere to put that energy — back into the supply (regenerative braking), into a resistor (dynamic braking), or into the motor's own losses (plugging, which is wasteful and thermally harsh).

"An overhead crane lowers a heavy load. Which quadrant is the drive in, and what happens to the energy?" — Quadrant IV: speed is negative (lowering) while torque stays positive (holding the load back). Gravity does the work, so the machine generates. That energy must go somewhere — returned to the supply by a regenerative converter, burned in a braking resistor, or the drive will see a rising DC-link voltage and trip.

Two conclusions that shape all EV design. First, cruising a car takes only about 10 kW — the 100 kW+ rating exists for acceleration and gradients, not for cruising. Second, at 90 km/h aerodynamic drag has already overtaken rolling resistance, and because it grows as v² the crossover moves the whole energy picture: doubling speed roughly quadruples the drag force and octuples the drag power.

Conventional Internal Combustion Engines (ICEs) suffer from severe thermodynamic and mechanical limitations: (1) zero static torque at zero RPM, requiring an idle speed (600–900 RPM) and a slipping friction clutch, (2) an extremely narrow thermal efficiency sweet spot (typically 25%–38% peak efficiency over a narrow speed-load envelope), and (3) complete inability to recapture kinetic energy during braking. Electric traction motors, conversely, produce full maximum torque from zero speed, operate at 90%–96% efficiency across broad speed-torque quadrants, and readily reverse power flow for regenerative braking.

In contrast, an electric traction motor delivers maximum constant torque from 0 to base speed (omega_b) (e.g., 0 to 4500 RPM), followed by a broad constant power field-weakening region extending up to maximum speed (omega_{max}) (e.g., 14,000–18,000 RPM). A speed ratio (omega_{max} / omega_b) of 3 to 4 allows a single-speed fixed-ratio reduction gearbox (typically (i_g cdot i_0 = 8:1) to (10:1)) to satisfy both maximum gradeability (launch acceleration) and top cruising speed requirements, eliminating synchronizers, clutch plates, shift solenoids, and 80% of driveline friction losses.

A semi-converter (half-controlled: two thyristors and two diodes instead of four thyristors) is cheaper and simpler, but it cannot produce negative output voltage — it has no inversion mode and therefore cannot regenerate. During the interval when the SCR conducts but the diode freewheels, the load current is diverted through a diode path instead of the supply, which improves the input current waveform and power factor compared with a full converter at the same firing angle, but at the cost of losing the fourth-quadrant capability.

A dual converter connects two full converters in anti-parallel across the motor, one firing to conduct positive current and the other negative, giving true four-quadrant operation without physically reversing any connections. In the circulating-current mode, both converters are kept gated on simultaneously (with their firing angles related by α₁ + α₂ = 180° so their average DC outputs match), and a reactor between them limits the resulting AC ripple current that circulates between the two bridges even when the load itself is not calling for a current reversal. The benefit is instant, bump-free reversal — the alternative, circulating-current-free operation, must detect the zero crossing and blank one converter before firing the other, which is simpler but slower to reverse.

In heavy industry, reversing the direction of motor rotation and recovering kinetic energy during deceleration (regenerative braking) is essential. A single converter only allows current to flow in one direction (due to the unidirectional conduction of thyristors). To achieve full four-quadrant operation without mechanical reversing contactors, two back-to-back connected converters—termed a Dual Converter—are employed. The dual converter can supply bidirectional armature voltage and bidirectional armature current with sub-cycle dynamic reversal times.
